catalog_quote: [p.46] The syllabic pattern of Pa-O language is basically monosyllabic. There are also a small number of disyllabic words and an even rarer number of trisyllabic and polysyllabic words. ... A monosyllabic word is a word with only one syllable. The strong stress usually occurs on that syllable. Its structure is ['s]. [p.47] This sub-type is composed of a presyllable which has an unstress followed by a major syllable. The strong stress is on the last syllable. Its structure is [u.'s]. [p.48] This sub-type is composed of two syllables The weak stress falls on the first syllable and the strong stress is on the last syllable. Its structure is [,w.'s]. ... A trisyllabic word is a word with three syllables, which is rare in Pa-O language. ... (I) [u.u.'s] ... (II) [u.,w.'s] ... (III) [,w.u.'s] ... (IV) [,w.,w.'s] [p.68] The stress in Huay Salop Pa-O dialect can be predicted from the syllable s…

new_statements.quote: p. 47: "This sub-type is composed of a presyllable which has an unstress followed by a major syllable. The strong stress is on the last syllable. Its structure is [u.'s]." p. 48: "The weak stress falls on the first syllable and the strong stress is on the last syllable. Its structure is [,w.'s]." p. 68: "The stress in Huay Salop Pa-O dialect can be predicted from the syllable structure. Therefore, the word stress is non-phonemic. There are three phonetic levels of stress: strong stress, weak stress, and un-stress" p. 72: "Stress is predictable by the syllable position in the phonological word and by the syllable structure: the final syllable in a phonological word is the major syllable" p. 108: "The strong stressed syllable occurs in monosyllabic word and in the last syllable of disyllabic and trisyllabic word while the weak stressed and the unstressed syllables can occur everywhere except at the end of the word."

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: All five quoted passages found verbatim at the stated locators (the scanned textbreaks only): p. 47 = PDF page 060, the scanned text 'This sub-type is composed of a presyllable which has an unstress followed by a major syllable. The strong stress is on the last syllable. Its structure is [u.'s].'; p. 48 = PDF 061, lines 2394-2395 '..The weak stress falls on the first syllable and the strong stress is on the last syllable. Its structure is [,w.'s].'; p. 68 = PDF 081, lines 3464-3467 'The stress in Huay Salop Pa-O dialect can be predicted from the syllable structure. Therefore, the word stress is non-phonemic. There are three phonetic levels of stress: strong stress, weak stress, and un-stres…
new_statements.relation_note: Catalog final stress (final) is exactly what the thesis describes for the Huay Salop dialect: strong stress on the last syllable of every 1-3 syllable word; refines with the secondary-stress/presyllable detail and the non-phonemic status.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary (strong) stress is non-phonemic and fully predictable: it falls on the major syllable, which is the only syllable of a monosyllable and always the last syllable of a disyllabic or trisyllabic phonological word (structures ['s], [u.'s], [,w.'s], [u.u.'s], [u.,w.'s], [,w.u.'s], [,w.,w.'s]). Stress is defined by intensity and vowel duration; tone (four tonemes) is the contrastive suprasegmental.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Weak (secondary) stress falls on any minor syllable (a full C(C)V(C)+tone syllable in non-final position); zero stress on the presyllable /Cə/. Both occur only in non-final positions (p. 69 'It occurs on any minor syllable'; p. 71 minor syllable 'always takes a secondary stress'; presyllable 'always takes a zero stress').
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the author says stress needs no marking in phonemic transcription because it is entirely predictable from position and syllable type. Words of 4-5 syllables are analysed as compounds or polysyllabic words with the same final-major-syllable pattern (p. 49-50).
new_statements.identity_note: Thanamteun (2000) describes the Pa-O (Taungthu) dialect of Ban Huay Salop, Tambon Huay Pha, Muang District, Mae Hong Son Province, Thailand (Northern Karen, Pa-O; ISO 639-3 blk), based on fieldwork with Thai-resident Pa-O speakers. It also summarises Jones (1961) on Taungthu in its literature review (pp. 18-19, PDF 31-32), which mentions stressed/unstressed allophones of tones and vowels but does not state a placement rule. The catalog entry is for Pa-O as a whole.

tone_statements.citation: Luangthongkum, Theraphan (2019). A view on Proto-Karen phonology and lexicon. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society (JSEALS) 12(1): i-lii. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press. hdl:10524/52441.
tone_statements.quote: His solution makes the PK tonal system look like that of some Modern Karenic languages which have four tones in non-checked or smooth syllables and two tones in the checked ones, such as Pa-O, Pwo, some varieties of Sgaw and so forth. ... The main distinction between the two varieties: (1) the phonetic characteristics of the B12 and B3 tones (<*B), i.e. B12 = 55, B3 = 53 in N.Pa-O but B12 = 33 and B3 = 55 in S.Pa-O; and (2) mostly, clear monophthongs in N.Pa-O while on-gliding and off-gliding vocalic quality plus a heavier phonation type in S.Pa-O due to the influence of Mon.
tone_statements.locator: p. iii, sec. 1 and p. vii, sec. 3; full tone boxes in Table 3 p. xii and Figure 4 p. xv
tone_statements.summary: Pa-O (N. and S. varieties, author's fieldwork): four tones in smooth syllables (N. Pa-O 31, 33, 55, 53; S. Pa-O 31, 53, 33, 55) plus two in checked syllables (21, 45), which fn. 4 (p. iii) treats as allotones of the high and low tones. Auditory transcription; 341-root lexicon with pitch numbers.

tone_statements.citation: Luangthongkum, Theraphan (2014). Proto-Karen (*k-rjaŋᴬ) fauna. MANUSYA: Journal of Humanities 17(3) [Special Issue 20]: 86-123. Bangkok: Chulalongkorn University (Brill-hosted). DOI 10.1163/26659077-01703006.
tone_statements.quote: Both of the Pa-O varieties have four tones in the smooth syllable and two tones in the checked syllable: 31̈ (A12), 33 (A3), 55 (B12), 53 (B3) and 21 (D12), 45 (D3) in Northern or Highland Pa-O; and 31̈ (A12), 53 (A3), 33 (B12), 55 (B3), 21 (D12) and 45 (D3) in Southern or Lowland Pa-O. This means that each of the proto-tones (*A *B *D) has split into two tones, i.e. *A > A12-3 or A1-23 *B > B12-3 and *D > D12-3 as shown in Figure 1 of the Appendix.
tone_statements.locator: section 'Tonal development', preprint p. 3; tone boxes for N. Pa-O and S. Pa-O in Appendix Figure 1 'Proto-Karen tones and tonal development in Modern Karen', preprint p. 30
tone_statements.summary: Own 2009-12 fieldwork: each Pa-O variety has 4 tones on smooth + 2 on checked syllables (six Chao values listed; n_tones counts all six), from a binary split of Proto-Karen *A *B *D. The '31' tone has a superscript diaeresis in print. Nothing on Pa-O stress; no acoustics.

sources.citation: Jitwiriyanont, Sujinat (2015). Gender variation in acoustic characteristics of Southern Pa-O lexical tones. MANUSYA: Journal of Humanities 18(2): 71-91. DOI 10.1163/26659077-01802004 (open access, via Internet Archive copy of Brill PDF).
sources.quote: No stress statement. Instrumental F0 study of 6 lexical tones (4 non-checked, 2 checked) of Southern (Thaton) Pa-O on 18 monosyllabic test words; phonological sketch gives 20 consonants, 11 vowels, 6 tones, no vowel-length contrast. Literature review p.72: 'There are a few linguistic studies on N. Pa-O (Jones, 1961; Burling, 1969; Thanamteun, 2000) ... Except for Thanamteun's study of N. Pa-O phonology, all studied Pa-O as part of Proto-Karen reconstruction.' Footnotes 1/3 identify the author's Chulalongkorn PhD on 'citation tones and tonal coarticulation in Pa-O continuous speech'.

sources.citation: Nishida, Tatsuo (1967 [vol. dated 1966 in Glottolog]). Biruma ni okeru Pao-zoku no gengo ni tsuite: Nanpō Pao-go Pa'an hōgen oboegaki [Notes on the Pao language in Burma: a preliminary study of the Southern Pao Pa'an dialect]. Gengo Kenkyū 50: 15-33. J-STAGE open.
sources.quote: No stress/accent statement (no occurrence of 強勢/アクセント/stress in the text). Describes Southern Pa-O (Pa'an) morphemes as monosyllabic CVC or disyllabic CV'CVC with a reduced glottal-checked first syllable (ka'tu 'head', ta'ka 'door', pa'li 'boat'), 4 tonemes (6 phonetic tone shapes), i.e. the same presyllable + full final syllable (sesquisyllabic) word shape that Thanamteun analyses as [u.'s]; consistent with, but not a statement of, final prominence.
